Justice Holmes · The Supreme Court · March 3, 1919

Schenck v. United States (1919)

Schenck v. United States, 249 U.S. 47. Opinion of the Court, delivered by Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., March 3, 1919. Text as published by the Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School. Legal citations omitted at the cuts marked [...].
Part 1

Before You Read

Chapter 1About This Source
Chapter 1

About This Source

Charles Schenck was the general secretary of the Socialist Party in Philadelphia. In 1917 the party printed thousands of leaflets and mailed them to men who had been called up for the draft. The leaflets argued that the draft was wrong and urged men to assert their rights. Schenck was convicted under the Espionage Act of 1917 of conspiring to interfere with the draft.

He appealed to the Supreme Court. He argued that the First Amendment protects freedom of speech and of the press. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., a Civil War veteran, wrote the opinion for a unanimous Court on March 3, 1919. The excerpt below describes the leaflet and states the Court’s reasoning.

The First Amendment says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press. Ask how the Court reads that sentence, and on what grounds it says the circumstances matter.

Part 2

The Leaflet

Chapter 2The Leaflet, in Plain English
Chapter 3The Leaflet, in the Original
Chapter 2

The Leaflet, in Plain English

Plain version, written for this page. These are not the Court's words.

The leaflet's first printed side quoted the first section of the Thirteenth Amendment. It said that the idea behind that amendment was violated by the conscription act, and that a conscript is little better than a convict. In passionate language it hinted that conscription was despotism in its worst form and a monstrous wrong against humanity, done in the interest of Wall Street's chosen few. It said, “Do not submit to intimidation,” but in form at least it stayed with peaceful measures, such as a petition for the repeal of the act.

Chapter 3

The Leaflet, in the Original

The original: the Court's description of the leaflet. [...] marks a cut.

The document in question upon its first printed side recited the first section of the Thirteenth Amendment, said that the idea embodied in it was violated by the conscription act and that a conscript is little better than a convict. In impassioned language it intimated that conscription was despotism in its worst form and a monstrous wrong against humanity in the interest of Wall Street’s chosen few. It said, ‘Do not submit to intimidation,’ but in form at least confined itself to peaceful measures such as a petition for the repeal of the act.

The Court's Reasoning

Chapter 4The Reasoning, in Plain English

Chapter 6A Note for You
Chapter 4

The Reasoning, in Plain English

Plain version, written for this page. These are not the Court's words.

Someone may say that even if the leaflet tended to obstruct the draft, the First Amendment to the Constitution protects it. The Court admits that in many places and in ordinary times the defendants would have been within their constitutional rights in saying all that the leaflet said. But the character of every act depends upon the circumstances in which it is done.

The Court gives an example. The strictest protection of free speech would not protect a man who falsely shouts fire in a theatre and causes a panic. It does not even protect a man from an injunction against words that may have all the effect of force.

The question in every case, the Court says, is whether the words are used in such circumstances, and are of such a nature, as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent. It is a question of proximity and degree. When a nation is at war, many things that might be said in time of peace are such a hindrance to its effort that they will not be endured as long as men fight, and no Court could regard them as protected by any constitutional right.

Chapter 5

The Reasoning, in the Original

The original: the Court's reasoning. [...] marks a cut.

But it is said, suppose that that was the tendency of this circular, it is protected by the First Amendment to the Constitution. [...] We admit that in many places and in ordinary times the defendants in saying all that was said in the circular would have been within their constitutional rights. But the character of every act depends upon the circumstances in which it is done. [...] The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic. It does not even protect a man from an injunction against uttering words that may have all the effect of force. [...] The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent. It is a question of proximity and degree. When a nation is at war many things that might be said in time of peace are such a hindrance to its effort that their utterance will not be endured so long as men fight and that no Court could regard them as protected by any constitutional right.

Chapter 6

A Note for You

From the page

Pay close attention to the phrases that set a standard: “clear and present danger” and “proximity and degree.” Notice also which facts about the leaflet the Court stresses, and which facts about the country the Court stresses. You can return to this page as often as you like.
